newsitem.title: USA: Albright cautions Russia on NATO issue.
newsitem.headline: Albright cautions Russia on NATO issue.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Wednesday launched a campaign for Senate support on enlarging NATO, ruling out compromise on key Russian demands over its ties with an expanded alliance.
Albright said she would go to Moscow next week to address outstanding differences, which include Russian demands for restrictions on the build-up of forces in new NATO members.

"Russia would ... like us to make absolute commitments in the (proposed Russia-NATO) charter about the deployment of nuclear and conventional forces on the territory's new members," she told the Senate Armed Services Committee.
"But we will not compromise on this issue," she said.
Albright said NATO would like an agreement to sign in Paris on May 27 formalising future relations between Moscow and the alliance, as Russia has suggested.

President Boris Yeltsin raised expectations when he said last week he would be ready to sign the charter then. But U.S. officials said Russia's demand for binding guarantees remains a stumbling block that Albright will discuss May 1 in Moscow.
The decision on new members, most likely Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, will be made formally at a summit of NATO's 16 leaders in Madrid in July.

Moscow wants commitments that the new members will not upgrade their military facilities to bring them in line with other NATO countries, and a pledge the alliance will "never" station nuclear weapons on the territory of new members.

Albright told the Senate panel: "All we have done and all we will do is to restate unilaterally existing NATO policy: that in the current and foreseeable security environment, we have no plan, no need and no intention to station nuclear weapons in the new member countries, nor do we contemplate permanently stationing substantial combat forces."

"The only binding limits on conventional forces in Europe will be set as we adapt the CFE (Conventional Forces in Europe) treaty, with central European countries and all the other signatories at the table," she said.

President Bill Clinton has taken the lead in pressing the alliance to take in its first new members since the Cold War ended and considers enlargement one of most significant foreign and defence policy issues of this era.
Senators said the issue will force a searching domestic debate about whether the United States should be willing to go to war for new members, the essence of NATO security vows.
Russia strongly opposes NATO expansion into its onetime Soviet Warsaw Pact allies but has come to accept that as inevitable and is pushing for the best deal it can get.
Defence Secretary William Cohen underscored that "NATO will not accept any limits on its infrastructure."

Testifying with Albright, he NATO's assertion of no plans to place nuclear weapons in new member states implies "the understanding that Russia would not place nuclear weaons on the territories of the former republics of the Soviet Union."
"And were they to do so this might very well cause NATO to reexamine" its own pledge, he said.
Albright said Clinton has been clear "about the lines we will not cross" as a new Russia-NATO partnership is formed.

This includes an insistence that enlargment will go forward regardless of whether a charter is agreed upon, no European nation will be excluded from potential NATO membership, new members will have full alliance rights and benefits and Russia will not have a veto in NATO affairs.
Increasingly Washington intellectuals have doubted the wisdom of enlargement, particularly its effect on Russia.

Albright countered that if it did not expand, "NATO would be stuck in the past, risking irrelevance, even dissolution. Our leadership in Europe will be compromised and relations with our traditional allies would deteriorate."

She and Cohen stressed the importance of Russia and NATO viewing each other in a non-adversarial post-Cold War light. But Cohen acknowledged that NATO, at essence, is a military alliance and Albright affirmed that the alliance would defend the west if Russia veers from its democratic course.

Cohen said expansion will cost new NATO members up to one billion annually. Existing NATO members would pay an extra $600-$800 million annually for regional reinforcement while direct expansion-related costs are about $900 million a year.
